sequences.title: State, dynamics, input and output
sequences.summary: Describe an inverted pendulum the way control theory does: a state that evolves, an input we choose and an output we measure.

initial.title: An inverted pendulum
initial.explanation: A rod balanced upright on a hinge. Its tilt from vertical, $\theta$, changes with time $t$. Before we can steer it we need a precise description of what it is doing.

steps.title: The state collects what we need to know
steps.explanation: The tilt $\theta$ alone does not tell us what happens next: a rod passing upright while swinging fast behaves differently from one at rest. Angle and angular velocity $\dot\theta = d\theta/dt$ together form the state vector $x$.

steps.title: A model predicts how the state changes
steps.explanation: A model gives the rate of change $\dot x$ from the current state. Followed forward in time it predicts the motion: upright is an equilibrium, but a tiny tilt grows and the rod falls. The upright position is unstable.

steps.title: Add an input we can choose
steps.explanation: Control adds an input $u$ that we set ourselves, for example a torque at the hinge or a motion of the base. The model now says how the state responds to both its own dynamics and to $u$.

steps.title: Measure an output
steps.explanation: Sensors report an output $y$ that depends on the state, perhaps only the angle. Later in this overview we assume the whole state is measured, $y = x$.

steps.title: State the goal
steps.explanation: With the upright position placed at $x = 0$, the control goal is to pick the input so the state returns to zero and stays near it, even though the uncontrolled rod would fall.

sequences.title: Types of control and the feedback loop
sequences.summary: From passive design to active control, open loop versus closed loop, assembled into a feedback block diagram.

initial.title: Ways to change behaviour
initial.explanation: There are many ways to make a system behave better. The overview sorts them by two questions: do we spend energy while it runs, and do we measure what it is doing?

steps.title: Passive or active
steps.explanation: Passive control is designed in once and needs no energy while running, like the streamlined tail fairing on a truck that reduces drag. Active control keeps putting energy in through an actuator.

steps.title: Active: open loop or closed loop
steps.explanation: Open-loop control plays a preplanned input without looking at the system. Closed-loop feedback uses sensors to decide the input. The book's diagram also lists disturbance feedforward: measuring an incoming disturbance and feeding it into a planned input.

steps.title: Open loop: plan the input from a model
steps.explanation: Given a desired output $r$, an open-loop controller uses a model of the system to compute the input $u$ that should produce it. Nothing flows back: if the model is wrong or something pushes the system, the controller never finds out.

steps.title: Closed loop: measure and feed back
steps.explanation: Now the measured output $y$ returns along the feedback path and is subtracted from the reference: the error $e = r - y$ drives the controller. The input reacts to what the system is actually doing.

steps.title: The overview's regulator
steps.explanation: For balancing, the reference is the upright state $r = 0$, every state is measured ($y = x$) and the controller is a gain matrix: $u = -Kx$. This is the loop analysed in the rest of the overview.

sequences.title: Why feedback?
sequences.summary: Four reasons from the lecture, each with the condition under which it holds.

initial.title: Why measure and feed back?
initial.explanation: Sensors, wiring and a control law add cost and complexity. The lecture lists four reasons they can be worth it. Each is a possibility that good design unlocks, not a guarantee.

steps.title: 1. Uncertainty inside the model
steps.explanation: A plan computed from a slightly wrong model (the rod a little taller, a car a little heavier) misses its target, and open loop cannot notice. Feedback measures the miss and corrects it without needing a perfect model.

steps.title: 2. Instability
steps.tex: \dot x = Ax + Bu(t):\ \text{eigenvalues of } A \text{ unchanged}
steps.explanation: Adding a preplanned input to a fixed linear model does not change $A$, so an eigenvalue at $\lambda = +1$ stays there. Feedback $u = -Kx$ makes the input depend on the state and changes the matrix itself, so it can move eigenvalues. (The vibrating-base pendulum works through a different, parametric effect.)

steps.title: 3. Disturbances from outside
steps.explanation: A gust of wind $d$ is external forcing that may be too hard to predict or measure directly. Its effect shows up in the measured output, so a well-designed feedback loop can counteract it. Uncertainty is internal (the model is wrong); disturbance is external.

steps.title: 4. Efficiency, and the fine print
steps.explanation: A good balancing controller acts early, so it needs only small corrections instead of constant pumping. But feedback is not automatically better: a poorly chosen gain can destabilize a loop, and high gain also amplifies sensor noise.

sequences.title: A static cruise-control teaching model
sequences.summary: Derive open-loop and proportional closed-loop speed for a deliberately crude static model.

initial.title: A crude static model
initial.explanation: A teaching model, not a vehicle simulator: speed $y$ responds instantly to throttle $u$ with gain $a$, plus a disturbance $d$ such as a hill. There are no dynamics, so it can show tracking error but not instability.

steps.title: Open loop: invert the model
steps.explanation: To reach the reference speed $r$, the open-loop plan inverts the model gain $a_m$. If the true gain $a$ differs from $a_m$, the speed is off by the ratio $a/a_m$, and the whole disturbance $d$ passes straight through.

steps.title: Closed loop: throttle from the error
steps.tex: u = K(r - y) \;\Rightarrow\; y = aK(r - y) + d
steps.explanation: A proportional controller opens the throttle in proportion to the speed error $r - y$. Substituting it into the model puts $y$ on both sides.

steps.title: Collect the $y$ terms
steps.explanation: Expand $aK(r - y)$, move $-aKy$ to the left and factor out $y$. Each step keeps exactly the same solutions.

steps.title: Solve and compare
steps.explanation: Divide by $1 + aK > 0$. The model mismatch is no longer needed and the disturbance is divided by $1 + aK$. With $a = 0.5$, $K = 50$: $y = \tfrac{25}{26}r + \tfrac{1}{26}d$. The error $(r - d)/(1 + aK)$ shrinks with gain but generally stays nonzero at finite $K$: proportional control alone cannot guarantee zero tracking error for every reference and disturbance.

sequences.title: The language of state space
sequences.summary: From $\dot x = Ax$ to $\dot x = Ax + Bu$, $y = Cx$, with the sizes of every matrix.

initial.title: A linear system
initial.explanation: Near an equilibrium many systems are well described by linear equations: each component of $\dot x$ is a fixed linear combination of the components of $x$, collected in the matrix $A$.

steps.title: The unforced solution
steps.explanation: The solution is the matrix exponential $e^{At}$ applied to the initial state. We will not compute it; what matters is that the eigenvalues of $A$ decide its behaviour: all real parts negative means decay to zero, any positive real part means growth.

steps.title: Add the control knob
steps.explanation: The input $u$ is the knob we turn: a motor voltage, a torque, the position of the base. The matrix $B$ says how each input component pushes the rate of change of the state.

steps.title: Measure with $C$
steps.explanation: Sensors read linear combinations of the state, $y = Cx$, possibly far fewer numbers than $x$ has. The general form adds $Du$; the overview assumes no direct feedthrough, $D = 0$.

steps.title: Check the sizes
steps.tex: x \in \mathbb{R}^n,\ u \in \mathbb{R}^m,\ y \in \mathbb{R}^p;\quad A_{n\times n},\ B_{n\times m},\ C_{p\times n}
steps.explanation: With $n$ states, $m$ inputs and $p$ outputs, $Ax$ and $Bu$ must both be $n$-vectors so they can be added to give $\dot x$, and $Cx$ is a $p$-vector.

steps.title: The pendulum in matrix form
steps.explanation: For the linearized, normalized inverted pendulum ($g/L = 1$, no damping), row times column gives $\dot\theta = \dot\theta$ (a bookkeeping row) and $\ddot\theta = \theta + u$: gravity amplifies the tilt and the torque $u$ pushes back.

sequences.title: Closing the loop: $A - BK$
sequences.summary: Substitute full-state feedback and factor the state out on the right.

initial.title: Controlled system, full state measured
initial.explanation: Assume every state is measured, $y = x$. A human balancing a broom has a good sense of both its angle and how fast it is moving, so this is a reasonable first model.

steps.title: Choose a feedback law
steps.explanation: Let the input be a fixed linear combination of the measured states: $u = -Kx$. Here $K$ is an $m \times n$ gain matrix, so $Kx$ has the size of $u$.

steps.title: Substitute
steps.explanation: Replace $u$ in the dynamics by $-Kx$. The input is no longer an outside signal: it is now determined by the state itself.

steps.title: Move the sign
steps.explanation: $B(-Kx) = -BKx$. Keep the order $B$ then $K$: matrix products do not commute.

steps.title: Factor $x$ on the right
steps.explanation: Both terms end in $x$, so factor it out on the right: $Ax - BKx = (A - BK)x$. $BK$ is $n\times m$ times $m\times n$, an $n\times n$ matrix like $A$. Writing $x(A - BK)$ or $A - KB$ would be wrong.

steps.title: The closed-loop matrix decides stability
steps.explanation: The closed loop is again $\dot x = A_{\text{cl}}x$, so the eigenvalues of $A - BK$, not of $A$, decide stability. All real parts negative: asymptotically stable. Any positive real part: unstable. Eigenvalues on the imaginary axis need further analysis.

sequences.title: Moving the pendulum's eigenvalues
sequences.summary: The book's example: $K = [4\ \ 4]$ moves the eigenvalues from $\pm 1$ to $-1$ and $-3$.

initial.title: The normalized pendulum and a gain
initial.explanation: The linearized upright pendulum with $g/L = 1$ and no damping, a single torque input, and the gain from Brunton & Kutz (printed p. 328): $u = -4\theta - 4\dot\theta$.

steps.title: Open-loop eigenvalues
steps.explanation: Without feedback the eigenvalues are $+1$ and $-1$: a saddle. The $+1$ in the right half-plane means almost every small tilt grows like $e^{t}$.

steps.title: Compute $BK$
steps.explanation: A column ($2\times1$) times a row ($1\times2$) is a $2\times2$ matrix: entry $(i,j)$ is $B_i K_j$. Only the second row is non-zero because the torque acts only on $\ddot\theta$.

steps.title: Subtract: $A - BK$
steps.explanation: Subtract entry by entry. The closed loop reads $\ddot\theta = -3\theta - 4\dot\theta$: a restoring spring and damping created by feedback.

steps.title: Characteristic polynomial
steps.explanation: For $\lambda I - A_{\text{cl}} = \begin{bmatrix}\lambda & -1\\ 3 & \lambda + 4\end{bmatrix}$ the determinant is $\lambda(\lambda+4) - (-1)(3)$. It factors with roots $-1$ and $-3$.

steps.title: The eigenvalues move
steps.explanation: Both closed-loop eigenvalues are in the left half-plane, so the linearized closed loop is asymptotically stable: a small tilt now decays instead of growing. This holds for the small-angle model; large tilts need the nonlinear equations.

steps.title: Recap and what comes next
steps.tex: \dot x = Ax + Bu,\ \ u = -Kx \;\Rightarrow\; \dot x = (A - BK)\,x
steps.explanation: Model, feedback law, closed-loop matrix, eigenvalues. Next in the bootcamp: when can $K$ place the eigenvalues anywhere (controllability), how to choose $K$ well (LQR), and what to do when only $y = Cx$ is measured (estimation, the Kalman filter).
